title: A Glossary of Automotive Industry Supply Chain Management Terms
summary: A glossary of automotive industry supply chain management terms, grouped by where each one sits in the flow from product design to payment.
body_markdown:
# A Glossary of Automotive Industry Supply Chain Management Terms


By[Peter Spaulding](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/peter-spaulding) , *Sr. Content Writer*


Last Updated August 20, 2026


7 min read


In this article, learn about:


- The four groups these terms fall into, and why grouping beats alphabetizing


- What a bill of materials is, and how the design and build versions differ


- How just-in-time production and Kanban work together on a plant floor


- The order documents industrial and automotive buyers expect, plus more supplier education on[The Supply Chain Source](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/)


Automotive industry supply chain management comes with its own vocabulary, and most of it arrives at once. A supplier new to the category hears bill of materials (BOM), just-in-time (JIT), Kanban, original equipment manufacturer (OEM), electronic data interchange (EDI), and advance ship notice (ASN) in the first week, usually in a meeting where everyone else already knows the words.


Most glossaries answer that with an alphabetical list. That works for a single lookup and not much else, because these terms are not independent. They are checkpoints in one flow that starts with a design and ends with a payment. The terms below are grouped by where they sit in that flow, so the definitions explain each other.


## Design and Planning Terms


This group of terms centers around the materials needed for each automotive product. Purchase volumes and production schedules are built from these documents.


- **Bill of materials (BOM):** The list of every raw material, component, and instruction needed to build a product.[PTC’s bill of materials explainer](https://www.ptc.com/en/blogs/plm/what-is-bom) calls it the full set of inputs a product requires. Engineering, purchasing, and finance all us this document for different reasons.[NetSuite’s BOM guide](https://www.netsuite.com/portal/resource/articles/erp/bill-of-materials-bom.shtml) adds that teams keep single-level and multi-level versions for different stages of development.


- **Engineering bill of materials (EBOM):** The design view. It lists parts and assemblies the way engineering drew them, and a new version appears each time the design changes.


- **Manufacturing bill of materials (MBOM):** The build view. It covers every item and sub-assembly needed to make a finished, shippable product, ordered by how the product goes together rather than how it was drawn.


## Production Control Terms


This group answers when parts arrive and how the floor asks for more. Both terms came out of automotive manufacturing, and they work as a pair.


- **Just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing:** A model where items get made to meet demand instead of in surplus or ahead of need.[TechTarget’s JIT explainer](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/just-in-time-manufacturing-JIT-manufacturing) names the goals as higher efficiency, lower cost, and faster delivery. It only works when suppliers are reliable and the buyer can see what is coming.


- **Kanban:** The signal that tells an upstream station or supplier to replace what was just used.[Planview’s guide to JIT and Kanban](https://www.planview.com/resources/articles/lkdc-jit-kanban/) describes Kanban as a scheduling and visual management method, not an inventory control system on its own. Toyota built it to make just-in-time flow visible, which is why the two terms travel together in auto plants.


**Related Reading:**[Inventory Optimization for Raw Materials: How Manufacturers Balance Resilience with Working Capital](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/inventory-optimization-for-raw-materials-how-manufacturers-balance-resilience-with-working-capital)


## Trading Partner Status Terms


This group answers whose requirements apply to you. The same part can move through two channels, with different qualification steps and paperwork on each.


- **Original equipment manufacturer (OEM):** The company that builds the finished vehicle or machine. An OEM part is made by or for that company to its own spec, so it matches what left the assembly line.


- **Aftermarket:** The channel for replacement parts made by other companies. Aftermarket parts are easier to source and vary more in quality, and they sell after the machine is already in service.


- **Tiered supplier:** Where a supplier sits relative to the OEM. A Tier 1 supplier sells straight to the OEM, a Tier 2 supplier sells to Tier 1, and the count continues down the chain.


That status drives qualification steps, part numbering, and the way a buyer expects to trade data.


**Related Reading:**[A Supply Chain Lexicon: Navigating Modern Trading Partnerships](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/a-supply-chain-lexicon-navigating-modern-trading-partnerships)


## Data Exchange Terms


This group answers how an order reaches you and how a shipment gets checked at the other end. These are the documents[industrial and automotive buyers](https://www.spscommerce.com/industries/automotive-supplies/) read, and the ones that cause chargebacks when the data is wrong.


- **Electronic data interchange (EDI):** The automated exchange of business documents between two companies’ systems.[The SPS Commerce guide to EDI](https://www.spscommerce.com/what-is-edi/) explains that each document gets converted to a standard format and processed with no manual entry, so an exchange that once took days finishes in minutes.


- **Purchase order (PO):** The buyer’s order for goods. In EDI it is the 850, and it carries the items requested, quantities, pricing, and shipping instructions.


- **Advance ship notice (ASN):** What a supplier sends once a shipment leaves before it lands. In EDI it is the 856.[The SPS Commerce guide to the EDI 856](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-856-advance-shipping-notice/) lists what it holds: quantities, UPC codes, pallet and carton configuration, plus ship-to and ship-from details. Most buyers want it before the truck shows up.


- **Invoice:** The supplier’s request for payment, sent as the EDI 810. The buyer matches it against the purchase order and the ASN before paying, so a mismatch in any of the three holds up the money.


- **Enterprise resource planning (ERP) system:** The system of record for orders and inventory. Linking EDI to the ERP is what ends manual re-entry.[SPS Commerce guidance on ERP projects](https://www.spscommerce.com/blog/successful-erp-implementation/) recommends making that link before an ERP rollout, so the data flow gets tested as part of the same project.


## What the Flow Looks Like on a Single Order


In sequence, the terms trace one order through all four stages.


1. Engineering releases the design, and the bill of materials lists what the product needs.


2. The buyer sends a purchase order, which arrives as an EDI 850 and lands in the ERP.


3. Production schedules the work. Under just-in-time, materials arrive as they are needed, and Kanban signals each replacement.


4. The shipment leaves, and the advance ship notice tells the dock what is coming and how it is packed.


5. The invoice follows, and the buyer matches it against the purchase order and the ASN before paying.


Each step leans on the one before it, which is why these terms are worth learning together.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What Is an OEM, and How Is It Different From Aftermarket?


OEM stands for original equipment manufacturer, the company that builds the finished vehicle or machine. An OEM part is made by or for that company to its own spec. A part made by a third party for the replacement market is aftermarket.


### What Is the Difference Between an EBOM and an MBOM?


The engineering bill of materials describes the product as designed, grouped by function. The manufacturing bill of materials describes it as built, grouped by assembly order, including the sub-assemblies needed to ship a finished unit.


### Is Kanban the Same Thing as Just-in-Time Manufacturing?


No. Just-in-time is the production model, which means making items to meet demand rather than stockpiling them. Kanban is the signaling method that keeps the model running on the floor. Plants adopt Kanban alongside JIT rather than in place of it.


### Which EDI Documents Do Industrial and Automotive Buyers Ask For First?


The purchase order (850), the advance ship notice (856), and the invoice (810) are the core set. Buyers reconcile all three against each other, so accuracy across the group matters more than any single document.


## Where To Go Deeper on Industrial and Automotive Supply Chain Terms


Definitions get you through the first meeting. The parts of the flow that get hard in practice, such as EDI compliance and ASN accuracy, take longer.


For suppliers looking to go deeper,[The Supply Chain Source](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/) publishes practical education on those topics, written for the people doing the work. If data exchange is the stage you need next, the[complete beginner’s guide to EDI](https://www.spscommerce.com/what-is-edi/) is a good place to start.
